clue.text: Rock music?

parts.note: rock is read as the gentle swaying of a baby, not the loud genre, so the music is what lulls an infant to sleep

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like the guitar genre, but here it means to rock a baby gently.
explanation.definitionFit: A lullaby sung while rocking a baby in its crib is exactly this kind of tune.

clue.text: Officer's custom, to share quarters

parts.note: CO is short for commanding officer
a habit is a custom or usual practice

explanation.surface: A soldier explains that it is the commanding officer's custom to share his living quarters.
explanation.definitionFit: To live together under one roof, especially as a couple, is to share living space.

clue.text: Combative GIs getting involved with action

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters of the two words around it are mixed together

explanation.surface: Soldiers who get drawn into action become aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting involved' tells you to jumble GIS and ACTION together.
explanation.definitionFit: Agonistic behaviour is competitive or argumentative, from the Greek for a contest.

clue.text: Bequeath, properly, a pound to someone? Don't interfere

parts.note: to bequeath is to leave something in a will
done properly means done well
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra
one can stand for a person, as in 'one does one's best'

explanation.surface: Advice about writing a will properly, leaving a pound to somebody, ends with a warning to keep out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom tells someone to let a situation be and not meddle with it.

clue.text: Fine outline we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word that follows is a sound-alike, judged by ear rather than spelling

parts.note: a summary is a brief outline of the main points

explanation.surface: Someone listens to a description of the general plan and approves it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like approval, but it describes the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine, warm, sunny weather is typical of the hottest season of the year.

clue.text: Puzzle that's nothing if not negative

parts.note: non, the French and Latin-derived word for no, is read as nothing at all
a quantity that is not negative is a plus, the opposite of minus

explanation.surface: A riddle is described as either worthless or at least not a minus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puzzle' is a verb here: to baffle someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To baffle or perplex someone so they are lost for what to say.

clue.text: Some Socialists turned back outside the Ministry

indicators.note: turned back says the run of letters found is then read in reverse order
some means only part of the following word is used, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: Some left-wingers have done an about-face, leaving the government department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' picks CIAL out of SoCIALists; 'turned back' reverses it. 'The Ministry' here is the church's ministry, the clergy, not a government department.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay people stand apart from the clergy, so they are outside the church's ordained service.

clue.text: A game female is not getting engaged

parts.note: loo is an old card game

explanation.surface: A gamely woman stays single and won't get engaged to anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engaged' suggests marriage, but means taking part.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone distant and uninvolved keeps apart from others rather than joining in.

clue.text: Pretender drops one, making a lot of noise

indicators.note: drops says a letter is let fall from the word before it

parts.note: a pretender to a throne is a claimant to it
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A would-be king loses one supporter and makes a racket about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drops' removes I from CLAIMANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Clamant means loud and insistent, clamouring for attention.

clue.text: Philosopher with old-fashioned views giving address in W1

parts.note: George Berkeley was an Irish philosopher and bishop
a square is a person with conventional, old-fashioned views

explanation.surface: A traditionalist thinker gives his London address.
explanation.walkthrough: W1 is a central London postcode, covering Mayfair. 'Old-fashioned views' looks like a description of the philosopher, but it gives SQUARE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mayfair garden square is a well-known location in London's W1 postal district.

clue.text: Central characters in schools that create a fuss

indicators.note: the central characters of a word are its middle letters, taken here from each of two words

explanation.surface: The main players in schools are the ones who cause trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central characters in' takes HOO from the middle of sc-HOO-ls and HA from t-HA-t.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-ha is a commotion or noisy row over something.

clue.text: Maine's not so unusual a state

indicators.note: so unusual says the letters are put in an odd new order

parts.note: Maine's taken with its S as written

explanation.surface: Maine is said to be quite an ordinary American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so unusual' tells you to rearrange MAINES and NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnesota is one of the fifty US states, in the upper Midwest.

clue.text: Beer will spill out of old copper jug

indicators.note: out of says the jumbled letters are formed around the coin
to spill something is to scatter it, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: D was the abbreviation for an old penny, a copper coin in pre-decimal money

explanation.surface: Beer is about to slosh out of an antique copper jug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jug' is slang for prison; Bridewell was a London house of correction whose name became general for a jail. 'spill' and 'out of' are the signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal for a prison, a place where offenders are locked up.

clue.text: Rex — alias protecting female novelist

parts.note: rex is Latin for king, abbreviated K

indicators.note: protecting means wrapping round, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: AKA stands for also known as, an alias

explanation.surface: A man named Rex uses a pseudonym to shield a woman writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'protecting' puts F inside AKA.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Kafka, author of The Trial, was a Prague-born writer of novels.

clue.text: Animal put in the yard, initially, not stable

indicators.note: put in says one piece is placed inside another
initially means the first letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: an otter is a river animal

explanation.surface: An animal kept in the yard is wobbly on its feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives T and Y; 'put in' puts OTTER between them. 'stable' looks like a noun for the animal, but means steady.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unsteady and wobbling is liable to fall, like a shaky old table.

clue.text: Petition, thus, not against the law

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
licit means lawful, the opposite of illicit

explanation.surface: Someone says that a petition is perfectly legal.
explanation.definitionFit: To solicit is to ask earnestly for something, just as a petition is a formal request.

clue.text: Hang up, having narrowly averted disaster

definitions.meaning: to hang up the phone is to end a conversation on the line
a near miss or narrow escape from danger

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang up' read literally means to bring a telephone conversation to an end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ending a phone conversation, and also a near miss, a narrow escape from danger.

clue.text: Rural company appearing in club I organised

indicators.note: appearing in says one piece shows up inside another
organised means arranged, so the letters are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A country business is advertised in a club the speaker has set up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' makes BULIC; 'appearing in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucolic describes pastoral countryside life, with shepherds and farms.

clue.text: Piece of lab equipment giving inventor a shock

parts.note: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone
a jar is a sudden jolt or shock

explanation.surface: A scientific device delivers an electric shock to its inventor.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass dome used in laboratories to cover apparatus or hold a vacuum.

clue.text: Do better upriver for fish

parts.note: to cap something is to outdo or top it
the river is the Nile, read upwards in this down entry, giving its letters backwards

explanation.surface: An angler moves upstream to improve their catch.
explanation.walkthrough: The single word 'upriver' does two things: river means NILE, and up reverses it to ELIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Capelin is a small silvery fish of northern seas, related to smelt.

clue.text: Male youth

parts.note: youth read as the period of being young, here the young years of a male

explanation.walkthrough: 'Male youth' looks like a young man, but here youth means a period of life.
explanation.definitionFit: The years a man spends as a lad, before adulthood, are his early years.

clue.text: Poison I place inside crate

indicators.note: inside says these letters go within another word

parts.note: bane is an old word for poison, as in henbane
PL is the abbreviation for place, as in street names

explanation.surface: A poison is hidden in a packing crate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crate' is slang for an old aircraft, not a box; 'inside' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Crate is old slang for a rickety aeroplane, and an early twin-winged plane fits.

clue.text: Rank, in this country, held by distinguished leader on the way up

indicators.note: held by means kept inside, so one piece sits within the other
the leader of a word is its first letter
up in a down entry says the letters are read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: a mode is a way of doing something
UK stands for the United Kingdom, the country of the newspaper

explanation.surface: A title in Britain is held by an eminent leader on his way up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' takes the first letter; 'up' reverses, as this is a down entry; 'held by' is the container signal. 'on the' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A dukedom is the title and status of a duke, the highest rank of peerage.

clue.text: Even if reversed, it makes no difference

indicators.text: if reversed, it makes no difference
indicators.note: the clue says turning the word round leaves it the same, so it reads identically both ways

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Someone notes that turning something round changes nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Even and flat surfaces are smooth, with no bumps or slope.

clue.text: Spectacular sixes by England's tail-ender

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral six, and two of them make sixes

indicators.note: the tail-ender is the last letter of a word

explanation.surface: A cricketer's batting is dazzling, hitting sixes as England's last man in.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a six is the biggest hit, and a tail-ender is a weak batsman near the end of the order; here it means the last letter, D.
explanation.definitionFit: Something vivid is bright and striking, which a spectacular show is too.

clue.text: Nonentity has narrow escape, put on the spot

parts.note: a pip is a spot, as on dice or playing cards
a squeak is a narrow escape, as in a near squeak

explanation.surface: An unimportant person narrowly escapes but is then put on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across entry, one piece 'put on' another is written after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipsqueak is a small, insignificant person of no importance.

clue.text: Poems by 19 ac, for example

parts.note: the cross-reference names the early years of life, so the poems are those written while young

explanation.walkthrough: The 19 across entry means the early years of a boy's life, so these are works from a writer's youth.
explanation.definitionFit: Juvenilia are the works an artist or writer produced while young.

clue.text: Give top mark — room for improvement after that?

parts.note: A is the top grade in an exam
a hospital ward is a room where patients get better

explanation.surface: A teacher hands out the best grade, then adds that there is still room for improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'room for improvement' looks like a teacher's comment, but means a hospital ward where patients improve.
explanation.definitionFit: To award a prize or grant is to give it formally.

clue.text: Oddly rounded fish

indicators.note: oddly means taking the letters in odd positions, first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.surface: A fish is described as strangely plump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' takes the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of rounded: R, U, D, D.
explanation.definitionFit: The rudd is a European freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: A bullet men developed before outbreak of hostilities

indicators.note: developed means worked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Soldiers developed a new bullet before the war broke out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developed' tells you to rearrange A BULLET MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Antebellum is Latin for before the war, used especially of the American South before the Civil War.
